Oct 8, 2026, 11:35 AM ET
New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
More Recent News
Oct 8, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays closer Bryan Baker shut the door in his team's 4-3 win over the New York Yankees in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with two strikeouts. Baker was a key part of Tampa Bay's three-game sweep of New York, logging saves in all three games while allowing just one baserunner to reach. The 31-year-old emerged as one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts and 41 saves across 62 1/3 innings (65 games). Heading into the American League Championship Series, Baker's dominance at the end of games gives Tampa Bay a significant advantage if it can get an early lead on its opponents.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Jakob Marsee Having UCL Repair With Internal Brace


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:24 AM ET
Miami Marlins outfielder Jakob Marsee (elbow) will get a UCL repair with an internal brace of his left elbow on Monday, according to Christina De Nicola of MLB.com. The estimated return-to-play timeline for Marsee is around six months. Marsee battled through elbow issues down the stretch in 2026 in his first full season in the majors with Miami. In his first taste of the big leagues in 2025, Marsee hit .292 (61-for-209) with five home runs, 33 RBI, 14 stolen bases, and 28 runs scored in 55 games and 234 plate appearances. In 155 games and 616 plate appearances this year, Marsee slashed .231/.348/.359 with a .706 OPS, 11 home runs, 41 RBI, 23 stolen bases, and 83 runs scored for the Fish. The 25-year-old former sixth-round pick by the San Diego Padres in 2022 from Central Michigan University has a very intriguing power/speed profile as an outfielder in all fantasy leagues, but his availability for Opening Day in 2027 could be in question, depending on how he fares during his rehab after going under the knife early next week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Oct 8, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Milwaukee Brewers outfielder Garrett Mitchell had a big game in his team's 3-1, series-clinching win over the San Diego Padres in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday. At the plate, Mitchell went two-for-four with a triple, an RBI, and a run scored. In the field, Mitchell robbed Padres third baseman Manny Machado of what would have been a game-tying two-run home run in the eighth inning. The 28-year-old Mitchell was finally able to stay mostly healthy in 2026, hitting .262/.354/.416 with 11 home runs, 65 RBI, 74 runs scored, and 14 stolen bases across 531 plate appearances in the regular season. He was productive in the NLDS as well, logging four hits, three runs scored, an RBI, and a stolen base across 15 at-bats.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Hagen Smith Opening Game 4 of ALDS on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Chicago White Sox rookie left-hander Hagen Smith will serve as the opener in Game 4 of the American League Division Series on Thursday at home against the division-rival Cleveland Guardians, according to Scott Merkin of MLB.com. The 23-year-old former fifth overall pick in 2024 from the University of Arkansas made 18 appearances (only one start) in his major-league debut during the 2026 regular season, posting a nice 1.29 ERA (2.35 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP with 41 strikeouts and 16 walks in 28 innings pitched. The talented young southpaw has already thrown 6 1/3 innings in his first experience in the playoffs, too, allowing just one earned run on three hits while walking five and striking out six. He started Game 1 of the ALDS against Cleveland and threw 2 2/3 shutout innings with three walks and four strikeouts in the team's 3-0 victory before allowing a run with two walks and a strikeout in two-thirds of an inning in Wednesday's Game 3 loss. Smith will probably have a short leash as the White Sox try to close out the best-of-five series, with right-hander Erick Fedde potentially piggybacking Smith in Chicago. In three relief appearances against the Guardians during the regular season, Smith allowed two earned runs with six walks and eight strikeouts in 5 2/3 innings pitched.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Scott Merkin
Victor Mesa Jr. Homers in ALDS-Clinching Win


Will Brady




Oct 8, 2026, 11:14 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. was one of the stars of his team's 4-3 win in Game 3 of the American League Division Series over the New York Yankees, hitting a two-run home run off Yankees left-hander Max Fried. Mesa Jr.'s home run was his only hit of the night, but it gave the Rays a 4-2 lead in the sixth inning that they would ultimately never give back. Across 262 plate appearances in the regular season, Mesa Jr. hit .260/.327/.498 with 14 home runs, 34 RBI, 37 runs scored, and nine stolen bases. After starting the year in the minors, the 25-year-old has emerged as an everyday corner outfielder for Tampa Bay and provides another dynamic power/speed bat for the Rays. If Mesa Jr. can get hot, he could help power a deep postseason run.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 10:01 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers closer Edwin Diaz picked up his second save in as many nights on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with a strikeout in his team's 4-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series. Diaz missed most of the 2026 regular season due to elbow and neck injuries. However, he's been dominant since returning from the injured list in mid-September. Diaz allowed just two baserunners while notching nine strikeouts in his final five innings pitched of the regular season, and he's now logged low-stress saves in each of his first two appearances of the playoffs. With Diaz rounding into form, Los Angeles' bullpen looks like a major strength heading into the National League Championship Series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:52 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians left-hander Foster Griffin was dominant in a bulk relief appearance in his team's 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Griffin followed Cleveland opener Daniel Espino and allowed two hits and one earned run while striking out seven across 2 2/3 innings of work. The 31-year-old was used exclusively as a starting pitcher during the regular season, posting a 15-6 record with a 3.60 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, and 158 strikeouts across 172 2/3 innings (31 starts) split between the Guardians and the Washington Nationals. However, Griffin struggled mightily late in the year, pitching to a 5.05 ERA in the second half and a 6.87 ERA across 18 1/3 innings in September. If Griffin can rediscover his early-season form in a bullpen role, he could help Cleveland mount a comeback in the ALDS.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:43 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians outfielder Jo Adell had a big night in his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, going 2-for-4 with a walk and three RBI. With the game tied 1-1 in the third inning, Adell put the Guardians ahead for good with a three-run triple off of White Sox left-hander Hagen Smith. Across 660 regular-season plate appearances split between the Guardians and the Los Angeles Angels, Adell hit .240/.298/.401 with 23 home runs, 94 RBI, 70 runs scored, and five stolen bases. He was better with Cleveland than he was with Los Angeles, posting a .740 OPS across 204 trips to the plate after the Guardians acquired him at the trade deadline. Adell has notched a couple of key hits for Cleveland in the ALDS and now has four RBI across the first three games of the series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:32 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages had the key hit in his team's 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday, logging a go-ahead two-run single off Braves right-hander Robert Suarez in the seventh inning. Pages finished the game with two hits and two RBI in three at-bats. The 25-year-old was a critical piece of the Dodgers lineup during the regular season, hitting .274 with 23 home runs, 85 RBI, 75 runs scored, and 13 stolen bases. However, Pages struggled mightily during the Dodgers' run to the 2025 World Series, notching just four hits in 55 postseason plate appearances. After his big night on Wednesday, Pages has already logged four hits in just 15 plate appearances in the 2026 playoffs.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:19 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians right-hander Cade Smith was lights out to secure his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Smith entered the game in the eighth inning and recorded the final six outs, logging five strikeouts without allowing a single baserunner. The 27-year-old was one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, pitching to a 1.95 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 107 strikeouts and 41 saves across 74 innings (69 games). Smith has been dominant so far in the Division Series as well, as he's yet to allow a hit or a walk in his four innings of work. If Cleveland is going to mount a comeback in the series, it will likely need Smith to continue his dominance.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:11 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians third baseman Jose Ramirez was one of the stars of his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series. In five plate appearances, Ramirez recorded a double, a triple, a walk, two RBI, two runs scored, and a stolen base. With Cleveland leading 5-3 in the 8th inning, it was Ramirez's two-run triple that sealed the win for the Guardians and kept the series alive to see Game 4. The 34-year-old battled through injuries and underperformance in 2026, hitting .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs, 53 RBI, 71 runs scored, and 37 stolen bases across 544 plate appearances. Ramirez also got off to a slow start in the postseason, going hitless in his first eight trips to the plate against the White Sox. If Cleveland is going to rally all the way back from two games down in the ALDS, it will need Ramirez to stay hot in Games 4 and 5.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Robert Gasser Starting Game 4 of NLDS Against Padres


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:08 PM ET
Milwaukee Brewers left-hander Robert Gasser will start for the Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday night at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres, according to Brewers reporter Sophia Minnaert. It will be Gasser's first career postseason start after throwing 2 2/3 innings of relief in the playoffs for the Brew Crew last year. The 27-year-old southpaw went 5-5 on the season with a 3.87 ERA (4.24 FIP) and 1.19 WHIP with a career-high 103 strikeouts and 35 walks in 109 1/3 innings across 21 appearances (20 starts). The problem for Gasser is that he has not made a start in almost two weeks, so he could be a bit rusty. Manager Pat Murphy will surely have a short hook on the young left-hander as the Brewers look to close the best-of-five series out in San Diego. Gasser was outstanding down the stretch in 2026, allowing two earned runs or fewer in each of his last six starts, walking 12 and striking out 31 in 32 1/3 innings during that span. He did not face the Padres at all during the regular season, which could give him a bit of an advantage.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Sophia Minnaert
Mason Miller Back From the Paternity List for Game 4


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 8:03 PM ET
The San Diego Padres announced on Wednesday that they returned right-handed closer Mason Miller from the paternity list, taking the place on the National League Division Series roster of left-handed reliever Wandy Peralta. Miller blew a two-inning save in Game 2 of the series in Milwaukee against the Brewers and was then unavailable for the win in Game 3 at Petco Park on Tuesday night. It is great news for the Padres, who did not have left-handed high-leverage reliever Adrian Morejon on Tuesday due to a left-shoulder issue. The Padres had to go to Game 1 starter, right-hander Michael King, for the two-inning save with both Miller and Morejon unavailable. It is uncertain if Morejon will be able to pitch late in the game in another must-win contest on Wednesday in Game 4, but the Padres will at least have their stud closer back in the fold. The two-time All-Star was lights-out during the regular season, his first full season with the Friars, posting a 1.67 ERA (1.17 FIP), 0.900 WHIP, a career-high and league-high 38 saves, a career-high 129 strikeouts, and 26 walks in just 70 innings pitched. With their season on the line, expect manager Craig Stammen to be aggressive in his usage of Miller if Game 4 is close in the later innings, even though he showed command issues in the ninth on Sunday in Milwaukee.--Keith Hernandez

Miguel Rojas Not Worried About Back/Hip Injury


Keith Hernandez




Oct 7, 2026, 12:28 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran infielder Miguel Rojas (back, hip) said he felt some tightness in his left lower-back/hip area during a swing in Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday against the hosting Atlanta Braves before he was pulled mid at-bat, according to Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic. However, Rojas was not concerned about his availability for the rest of the series and going forward. Rojas probably will not be in the Dodgers' starting lineup for Game 4 of the series on Wednesday at Truist Park against Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle, but it sounds like he should be available off the bench. The 37-year-old Venezuelan infielder has made two starts so far in the NLDS against the Braves and has gone 1-for-4 with a double and a strikeout. He was hitless in three at-bats with a strikeout in Tuesday's Game 3 win before being replaced at second base by Tommy Edman. Rojas has mostly been a bench player for the Dodgers in his 13th year in the league (fourth with L.A.) in 2026, but he proved in last year's World Series that he is still capable of coming through in the clutch when needed. He hit .267 (60-for-225) with four homers and 23 RBI during the regular season.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Fabian Ardaya
Oct 7, 2026, 11:57 AM ET
St. Louis Cardinals right-handed closer Riley O'Brien was a first-time All-Star in 2026 in his first full season as the team's closer, and he ended the year tied with San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller for the National League lead in saves (38) with a 4.08 ERA across a career-high 64 innings pitched. O'Brien also set a career high in appearances (66) in his first full year as a big-leaguer. He did not allow an earned run in his first 13 appearances of the year and ended the first half with a 3.43 ERA and a 7.9% walk rate in 39 1/3 frames. O'Brien had 24 saves in his first 28 opportunities. But in 27 appearances after the All-Star break, O'Brien had a 5.11 ERA in 24 2/3 innings, and his walk rate rose to 14.4% while he went 14-for-18 in save chances. Three of his blown saves in the second half came in September, and five of his losing decisions came in his final 13 outings. The 31-year-old said he experienced "fatigue" in the closing days of the season and that his legs have "been feeling heavy compared to how they felt early in the year," according to Daniel Guerrero of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. As he tired, the velocity of O'Brien's pitches suffered. To be able to maintain velocity through the entire season, O'Brien said he plans to focus on putting on "as much muscle as I can."--Keith Hernandez

Curtis Mead the Favorite to Start at Second Base Next Year

Oct 7, 2026, 11:47 AM ET
Boston Red Sox infielder Curtis Mead is considered the favorite to open next season as the team's starting second baseman, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline this summer, but he ended up playing in only one game for Boston due to a fractured wrist that he suffered in his second at-bat with the team. The 25-year-old will now have all offseason to heal up, and he will enter spring training as the team's primary option at the keystone as they attempt to get back to the playoffs in 2027. The Australian native was having a breakout 2026 campaign with the Nationals before being traded to Boston, and he finished the year with a .253/.353/.498 slash line with an .851 OPS, 17 home runs, 48 RBI, 49 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 285 at-bats in 88 combined games with Washington and Boston. The Yankees offered Paul Goldschmidt a $4 million deal to play one more season in what certainly has looked like a Hall of Fame career. He accepted, even though he knew he would no longer be the every-day starter. The organization got a massive return on their investment as the first baseman hit 18 home runs and had 52 RBI in essentially a platoon role.
Goldschmidt was incredibly disappointed after the Yankees lost to Tampa Bay, 4-3, in the Game 3 of their AL Division Series on Wednesday night at the Stadium. But when asked about the notion of reprising the role one more time, he replied, “I'd like to continue playing, so we'll see if that opportunity happens.”
“I’ve absolutely loved my time here – I don't know if there's anyone who loved being a Yankee more than me,” Goldschmidt said. “I love the guys in this clubhouse. I love living here in New York. But you don't really know what the future holds so I think we'll just see what happens. But I can't say enough great things about this organization and my time here. We'll see what happens.”
Goldschmidt won the 2022 NL MVP Award with St. Louis and finished second in MVP voting two other times and third once while with the Diamondbacks. He has 390 home runs, an .877 OPS and four Gold Gloves for his defense.
He will be 39 next season.
Goldschmidt played in his first postseason in 2011 when he broke into the majors as Arizona lost to Milwaukee in the NL Division Series. He made the playoffs once more with the D-backs in 2017 and then three times with St. Louis from 2019 to 2021. He’s now made it twice with the Yankees but still has yet to win a World Series.
“My mindset really hasn't changed: hopefully be able to have a chance to do that again and hopefully win a championship,” he said.
Considered a good influence on the clubhouse and on the younger Yankees in particular, Goldschmidt was asked about what his message would be to the players who are beginning to form a nucleus for the years ahead.
“I think you’ve just got to keep working, but not taking this for granted either,” he said. “You don't know if you're going to get the opportunity again. You don't know what our individual careers hold. You don't know what team you'll be playing for the next year. . . . and that's what makes this so disappointing.
“But the young guys here did great. They’ve got a great head on their shoulders, very talented physically, but also mentally. They know what they're doing, and they've done a great job. Without those guys, we wouldn't be here right now. So the future is bright for them individually, and I think for this organization too.”

NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night.
Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx?
It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the Rays are still right where they want to be, holding a commanding 2-0 lead in the series with three chances to advance to the AL Championship Series.
“It's amazing, man. It's exactly the way we wanted to start the series,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “To be able to play in front of these fans in this building and take a 2-0 series lead was exactly what we wanted, so it feels really good right now.”
Maybe home-field advantage is what the Yankees need after coming up empty against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and kicking the ball around the infield in a mistake-filled Game 2 defeat. Or maybe it’ll help to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound, knowing how tough he’s been on Tampa Bay throughout his career.
“We've got to get over it,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Game 2. “We've responded all year to difficult times, and we've got to do that again. We've got to get ourselves up off the mat.”
Tampa Bay’s pitching staff held what looked like a red-hot New York lineup to only two runs in the first 18 innings of this series. If the Rays keep that up, they could enjoy another champagne-soaked night in the city that never sleeps.
“I think it's sweet either way. Doesn't matter the clubhouse,” Rays center fielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously, going over there, having the chance to do that would be pretty special.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Yankees-Rays Division Series is set for 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Nick Martinez, RHP
Key stats: 7-3, 2.38 ERA in 16 road starts this season
After rolling out Rasmussen in Game 1 and Freddy Peralta in Game 2, Martinez was the logical choice for the Rays with the series moving to the Bronx. The veteran right-hander was a reliable presence on the mound for Tampa Bay all season, as he posted a 3.10 ERA over 180 innings while the club went 22-9 in his starts. He was at his best on the road, including two outings in the Bronx. The first-time All-Star held the Yankees to only three runs over 12 innings in their home ballpark.
Yankees: Max Fried, LHP
Key stats: 5-1, 1.81 ERA in 7 career GS vs. Tampa Bay
Fried is coming off a sharp outing against the Red Sox in the decisive Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series, holding Boston to a run on three hits over six innings. Fried walked one and struck out six, his third postseason start since joining the Yankees.
This will be Fried’s third time facing the Rays this season. He last saw them on Sept. 22 in New York, taking the loss in a 6 2/3-inning effort as Tampa Bay clinched the AL East.
Fried also went up against the Rays on April 11 at Tropicana Field, taking a no-decision after permitting three runs over eight innings. For his career, Fried is 5-1 with a 1.81 ERA in seven starts vs. Tampa Bay, including 3-0 with a 0.84 ERA in three starts during the 2025 season.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Rays: It seems likely the Rays will change things up a bit against the Yankees’ left-handers, opting for the right-handed side of most platoons and leaving their lefty hitters available off the bench. Here’s one potential look for a more right-handed lineup.
Yankees: The Yankees have used the same lefty-heavy lineup three times this postseason against right-handed pitchers, including twice in the ALDS. Boone said he is considering shaking things up for Game 3. Boone said before Game 2 that he was considering starting Anthony Volpe at third base. Jose Caballero and Paul Goldschmidt could also enter the mix.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays really couldn’t be in much better shape thanks to their starting rotation. Rasmussen handled eight innings in Game 1, and the duo of Peralta and Ian Seymour combined to work 7 2/3 innings in Game 2. So, their traditional relievers have recorded seven of the 54 outs so far this series: six from Baker and a big one from lefty Cam Booser. They may not turn to Peralta or Seymour in Game 3, but they still have starter Griffin Jax available -- and the Yankees have yet to face setup men Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly in this series.
Yankees: Ryan Weathers replaced infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario for this series, returning from a left flexor strain sustained in late August. David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick should all be leaned upon for high-leverage outs. Will Warren is now in the bullpen after appearing in 32 games (29 starts) during the regular season. Warren made one appearance in the Wild Card Series, tossing 1 2/3 innings.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: Nothing new. Everyone who was expected to be available for this series is on the roster. The most notable injury situation to watch moving forward is that of left-hander Shane McClanahan, whose status is unclear except that he will not pitch in this series.
Yankees: Aaron Judge was left off the ALDS roster, though Boone said it was a “close” call. Judge has yet to run the bases as he recovers from a right calf strain, though he has been performing outfield running. He has also been taking numerous live at-bats while throwing. Clarke Schmidt has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Aranda doesn’t get as much love as the other members of the “Big Three,” but his left-handed bat is key. He hit better than either Caminero or Díaz in September, and he had the lone big hit of the night in Game 1 before picking up two more hits in Game 2. Richie Palacios finished strong, too, posting a .981 OPS with five homers in September before delivering the biggest hit of Game 2, and the Brooklyn native likes hitting against his hometown Yankees. Tampa Bay’s entire rotation surged into the postseason, highlighted by Rasmussen and Peralta, the September AL Pitcher of the Month.
The Rays’ outfield is off to a slow start in this series, offensively, but they all showed the impact they can have by putting the ball in play in Game 2. And their defense has been consistently excellent.
Yankees: Rice has been the Yankees' most productive hitter in the postseason, and given how the ALDS has gone, it hasn't been particularly close. Rice is 7-for-15 (.467) in the playoffs, including his two-homer performance in ALDS Game 2. Rice has four homers and eight RBIs overall. Wells is 5-for-12 (.417) in the playoffs, including a couple of doubles in the ALDS. Everyone except for Rice and Wells has combined to go 1-for-46 (.022) in the ALDS so far.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Yankees won four of the six games these clubs played in the Bronx during the regular season, splitting a pair of games in late May, then taking three of four the final week of the season. However, the Rays have already celebrated once at Yankee Stadium, as they clinched the AL East title with a 6-1 win in the second half of a doubleheader on Sept. 22.

The Yankees made MLB playoff history in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, starting eight true left-handed hitters to face right-handed Boston Red Sox starter Sonny Gray.
Never before had a team started that many lefty batters — not including switch-hitters — in a postseason game, per the Elias Sports Bureau.
“I saw our lineup and I assumed that was probably the case,” one of those lefties, Cody Bellinger, told the Daily News with a grin. “I didn’t know. We’ve got a lot of talent in this locker room.”
It was in stark contrast to Tuesday night’s Game 1, when the Yankees started only four left-handed batters against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle in an eventual 9-0 win in the Bronx.
On Wednesday night, lefty-swinging first baseman Luis García Jr., second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., center fielder Trent Grisham and third baseman Ryan McMahon all returned to the starting lineup as the Yankees sought platoon advantages.
Lefty-hitting Spencer Jones, who started Game 1 in center field, moved to right field for Game 2.
Meanwhile, righty-swinging Paul Goldschmidt, Heliot Ramos, Amed Rosario and Anthony Volpe all began Wednesday’s game on the bench after starting Game 1.
Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. was the only right-handed batter in Wednesday’s lineup.
Gray is actually a bit tougher against lefty batters than righties, but because the Red Sox carry five left-handed relievers, Boone said he liked having a bench full of right-handed batters that he could deploy in the later innings.
The best-of-three Wild Card Series allows for this kind of maneuvering because, given its short nature, teams are able to carry more hitters and be more aggressive with their bench moves.
The Yankees carried 16 position players in the Wild Card Series, compared to just 10 pitchers.
That likely won’t be the case in future rounds, when they would need to use a fourth starting pitcher and cover more innings with their bullpen.
But Games 1 and 2 against the Red Sox showed how the Yankees plan to approach the postseason, with matchups dictating their lineup decisions perhaps more than they have in the past.
“With this group, I feel like it’s going to take everyone,” manager Aaron Boone said Wednesday. “So that’s my plan — day in and day out, it’s going to be a little different, potentially. And that phrase ‘all hands on deck’ certainly applies to us with our team right now.”
The Yankees need to prioritize lineup creativity even more because the matchup-proof Aaron Judge is sidelined indefinitely with a calf strain.
Giancarlo Stanton — who also typically starts against righties and lefties — is currently relegated to pinch-hitting duty after missing more than five months due to three separate calf strains.
And Wednesday marked the first game started by Grisham since Sept. 4, when he suffered a hamstring strain. After being activated for the Wild Card round, Grisham entered Game 1 in the seventh inning as a defensive replacement and went 0-for-1 at the plate.
“I know he’s ready to go,” Boone said. “I liked his at-bat [in Game 1] when he came in, hit a ball well to center. I don’t know what I’m going to get from any of the guys tonight. But I’ve got a lot of confidence in who he is and what he can bring to the table.”
The Yankees became even more platoon-oriented after they acquired García and Ramos, both of whom perform to traditional splits, before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
All of those factors led to Wednesday’s historic, lefty-loaded lineup.
“It’s super beneficial for us, because all the guys in the lineup are super tight — righties and lefties — and there will be a lot of different conversations between different guys in what they saw, how they picked it up,” Jones told The News.
“And then we’ve got a bunch of guys ready to go off the bench.”
SCHMIDT SHUT DOWN
Clarke Schmidt’s season is officially over.
The right-hander has been shut down after landing on the IL with right biceps neuritis shortly after making his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery.
Boone said last week that it was his understanding Schmidt would be shut down, but he hadn’t confirmed it until Wednesday.
But Boone said Schmidt is doing “fine.” That’s in line with what Boone shared last week, when he said Schmidt was expected to have a normal winter to build up for spring training.
More than a year after undergoing elbow surgery, Schmidt made his season debut on Sept. 16 and recorded two outs in a relief appearance.
A starter by trade, Schmidt had hoped to help out of the Yankees’ bullpen this postseason.
But Schmidt experienced a cramping sensation as he warmed up for a second relief appearance, then returned to the IL last Thursday.
VOLPE NEWS
Volpe has a new agent, confirming to The News that he is now being represented by Scott Boras and the Boras Corporation.
Boras is baseball’s most prolific agent, representing stars such as Juan Soto, Gerrit Cole and Bellinger.
Volpe, 25, is eligible for free agency after the 2028 season.

The Red Sox paid a handsome price for former Orioles catcher Adley Rutschman at the MLB trade deadline, dealing a handful of top prospects for the former No. 1 overall pick. After a middling second half, Chad Tracy’s first playoff lineup decision as manager of the Red Sox puts a lot of faith in Rutschman.
Tracy unveiled the Red Sox starting lineup that would hit against Yankees ace and likely Cy Young Cam Schlittler in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card at Yankee Stadium. Unsurprisingly, former top overall prospect in baseball Roman Anthony is leading off, but it’s Rutschman batting second ahead of All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras in the #3 spot.
Rutschman’s place in the order had been messed around with in the final days of the regular season, with Rutschman batting second, third or fifth on a given night. Much of Rutschman’s batting second has to do with the loss of Mickey Gasper to a biceps injury, as Gasper was usually the guy Tracy wanted on base ahead of the Red Sox’ power bats.
Chad Tracy’s Informed Adley Rutschman Lineup Decision
The decision to bat Rutschman second isn’t arbitrary: Rutschman is one of just two Red Sox players currently to have an extra base hit against Schlittler this year, along with third baseman Caleb Durbin, who hit a two-run home run against him earlier this season.
The Red Sox’ starting nine of Anthony, Rutschman, Contreras, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Nick Sogard, Jarren Duran, Trevor Story and Durbin is just a combined 8-for-59 (.136) with the two extra base hits against Schlittler this season.
The lineup appears to be Chad Tracy’s best attempt at getting some runs across against Schlittler. The announcement comes amid musings that the Red Sox reportedly “wore out” the Rays’ Trajekt machine mimicking Schlittler’s arsenal this weekend while they were playing their season finale against the Cubs in the domed Tropicana Field due to heavy rain in Boston.
AL Wild Card Preview
The Yankees put out a platoon-heavy lineup of their own, starting veterans Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario over Luis Garcia Jr. at first and Jazz Chisholm Jr at second. The Yankees got a “mini break” as their games against the Orioles on Saturday and Sunday, with no clinching scenarios on the line, were canceled due to the same nor’easter that pushed the Sox and Cubs to Florida.
It’ll be a rematch of the 2025 American League Wild Card series, which the Yankees won in three electrifying games, but with a different cast of characters, Rutschman chief among them. The Red Sox will surely rely on him finding his bat this series after posting a disappointing .222/.278/.410 slash in the final two months of the season after the trade from Baltimore. He’ll be thrown immediately into the fire against Schlittler, and it should certainly be a fun one.

The New York Yankees are set to hit the postseason stage against their century long rivals the Boston Red Sox.
First pitch of their best-of-three American League Wild Card Game is scheduled for 8:00 P.M. EST at Yankee Stadium.
Yankees first baseman Paul Goldschmidt could join a small group in MLB postseason history, if he finds himself atop of the New York lineup.
Paul Goldschmidt Could Join Small Group Age 39+ to Bat Leadoff in Postseason Game
Ahead of the official lineups, many insiders and MLB reporters are predicting that Paul Goldschmidt will be batting leadoff against Boston Red Sox LHP Payton Tolle.
If true, Goldschmidt will make history as the seventh player 39 and older to bat leadoff in an MLB postseason game.
“If Paul Goldschmidt bats leadoff tonight, he will join the following group to do so in the postseason at 39+ years of age: Justin Turner ’25 Cubs, Craig Biggio ’05 Astros, Rickey Henderson ’00 Mariners & ’99 Mets, Ozzie Smith ’96 Cards, Joe Morgan ’83 Phillies, Pete Rose ’80 Phillies.”
Goldschmidt has been slotted in at the leadoff spot 41 games this season for the Yankees.
The 39-year-old is also slashing .299/.393/.573 with an OPS of .967 and 11 home runs against left-handed pitchers.
He is also is the organization’s best defensive first baseman, and could use his veteran presence on the field to start the game.
UPDATE: Paul Goldschmidt is officially leading off for the New York Yankees, cementing him in postseason history.
Paul Goldschmidt’s Career
Paul Goldschmidt is a 16-year MLB veteran, who has spent the last two seasons of his career as a New York Yankee.
In the regular season Goldschmidt is slashing .286/.375/.501 with 390 home runs and 1,284 RBIs.
Goldschmidt is a seven-time MLB All-Star, five-time Silver Slugger, four-time Gold Glover, two-time Hank Aaron award recipient, and the 2022 National League MVP.
In the postseason, Goldschmidt is slashing .277/.354/.564 with a .918 OPS with eight home runs and 16 RBIs in 29 games since 2011 with the Arizona Diamondbacks.
In the Yankees 2025 postseason run, Goldschmidt slashed .444/.545/.444 with a .989 OPS.

item.content:encoded:
Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

First baseman Pete Alonso of the Baltimore Orioles has been named the American League Player of the Week, and third baseman Nolan Arenado of the Arizona Diamondbacks has been selected the National League Player of the Week. The announcements were made earlier today on MLB Network.
Alonso earned the honor for the seventh time in his career and second time this season after winning his first award in the AL with the Orioles on August 17th. He previously won five times during his tenure with the New York Mets, including June 24, 2019; September 26, 2022; July 30, 2023; April 15, 2024; and June 9, 2025. Alonso is the 12th player ever to garner honors in at least five consecutive seasons, regardless of team or league, joining Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero (8 seasons, 1998-2005); Manny Ramirez (7 seasons, 1997-2003); Arenado (6 seasons, 2014-2019); Aaron Judge (6 seasons, 2020-2025); George Bell (5 seasons, 1986-1990); Miguel Cabrera (5 seasons, 2012-2016); Hall of Famer Andre Dawson (5 seasons, 1987-1991); Carlos Delgado (5 seasons, 2000-2004); Clayton Kershaw (5 seasons, 2011-2015); Albert Pujols (5 seasons, 2005-2009); and Gary Sheffield (5 seasons, 1992-96). Arenado earned his ninth career award and first as a member of the Diamondbacks, marking Arizona’s fourth award of the year in addition to his teammates Ildemaro Vargas (April 27th); Ketel Marte (May 26th) and Corbin Carroll (August 17th). Arenado previously won six times as a member of the Colorado Rockies between 2014-2019 and twice as a member of the St. Louis Cardinals in 2022, including August 24, 2014; June 28, 2015; April 18, 2016; July 24, 2017; June 25, 2018; May 27, 2019; April 11, 2022; and August 8, 2022. He is the 31st player with at least nine awards in his career and just the eighth with at least nine awards in the National League, joining Barry Bonds (15); Pujols (13); Hall of Famer Mike Piazza (12); Sammy Sosa (11); Freddie Freeman (10); Hall of Famer Tony Gwynn (10); and Sheffield (9).
- The 31-year-old hit .389 (7-for-18) with five homers, eight RBI, three walks, eight runs scored, a 1.222 slugging percentage and a .500 on-base percentage across five contests.
- The Tampa, Florida native led the Majors in homers, slugging, OPS (1.722) and total bases (22); ranked second in runs scored; tied for third in RBI; and tied for fifth in on-base percentage.
- The five-time All-Star opened his week with a two-homer game against the Blue Jays on Monday and hit a pair of longballs in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium on Friday. Alonso now has 29 career multi-homer games which are third-most in the Majors since his debut in 2019 behind only Aaron Judge (40 G) and Kyle Schwarber (36 G).
- The 2019 Jackie Robinson NL Rookie of the Year also slugged a home run in the first game of a doubleheader on Wednesday against Toronto as he finished his year with 43 homers and 113 RBI. Per Elias, he became the first player since RBI became official in 1920 to lead the AL and NL in RBI for a single season after he led the NL with 131 RBI in 2022. Additionally, he is the eighth Orioles player to lead the league in RBI and the first since Chris Davis had 138 RBI in 2013.
- The 2025 Silver Slugger crossed the 40-homer threshold with his two-homer game on Monday, marking his fourth season of at least 40 home runs, joining 2019 (53 HR); 2022 (40 HR); and 2023 (46 HR). His 43 homers are third-most by a Baltimore player in their first season with the club, behind Hall of Famer Frank Robinson (49 HR in 1966) and Mark Trumbo (47 HR in 2016). Alonso, who has played in 577 consecutive games since June 18, 2023, became the first Oriole to start every game of a season since Jonathan Schoop in 2016.
- The 35-year-old hit .435 (10-for-23) with three homers, eight RBI, two doubles, two walks, seven runs scored, a stolen base, a .913 slugging percentage and a .519 on-base percentage in six games.
- The Newport Beach, California native tied for second in total bases (21) and hits; ranked third in on-base percentage and OPS (1.432); tied for third in slugging, RBI and runs scored; and tied for fifth in batting average.
- The eight-time All-Star slugged a homer on Tuesday and Thursday at Colorado before also going deep on Friday at San Diego, marking his 30th homer of the year. It marked the eighth time in his career that he hit at least 30 homers, and his eight seasons of at least 30 home runs are third-most by a primary third baseman (min. 100 GS at 3B in season), behind only Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12 seasons of 30+ HR) and Eddie Mathews (10 seasons of 30+ HR).
- The 10-time Rawlings Gold Glover and six-time Platinum Glove Award winner finished his season on a 13-game hitting streak that dates back to September 13th, and he hit safely in 18 of his final 20 games of the season. During the stretch, he slashed .420/.463/.840 with six homers, 16 RBI and a 1.303 OPS. Arenado’s hitting streak is the fourth-longest by a Diamondbacks player to end a season, trailing only Paul Goldschmidt (19 G in 2013); Chad Tracy (14 G in 2005); and Tony Womack (14 G in 1999).
- The five-time Silver Slugger reached base safely in each of his last 21 games, matching Luis Gonzalez (2001) for the longest streak to end a season in franchise history. Overall, his 21-game on-base streak is the fifth-longest single season on-base streak of his career behind a 30-game streak in 2014, a 25-gamer in 2024 and a pair of 24-gamers in 2024 and 2018.
Other noteworthy NL performances last week included starting pitcher Jared Jones (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 2 GS, 11.0 IP, 2 H, 0 BB, 14 SO) of the Pittsburgh Pirates; starting pitcher Eury Pérez (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 1 GS, 10.0 IP, 1 H, 1 BB, 11 SO) of the Miami Marlins; infielder Bryson Stott (.474, 2 RBI, 6 2B, 5 BB, 4 R, .789 SLG, .583 OBP) of the Philadelphia Phillies; rookie outfielder Carson Benge (.440, 1 HR, 4 RBI, 3 2B, 3 BB, 5 R, .680 SLG, .500 OBP) of the New York Mets; second baseman Brice Turang (.360, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 3 2B, 1 BB, 5 R, .720 SLG) and outfielder Jackson Chourio (.471, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 3 BB, 7 R, 2 SB, .647 SLG, .550 OBP) of the Milwaukee Brewers; the 2026 Tony Gwynn NL Batting Champion, catcher Gabriel Moreno (.400, 1 HR, 8 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 2 BB, 5 R, .600 SLG, .435 OBP) of the Arizona Diamondbacks; and utilityman Mauricio Dubón (.368, 1 HR, 3 RBI, 1 BB, 3 R, 1 SB, .526 SLG, .400 OBP) of the Atlanta Braves.
Other noteworthy AL performances last week included rookie outfielder Lucas Spence (.333, 4 HR, 9 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 4 BB, 5 R, 1.167 SLG, .455 OBP), the 2026 AL Rod Carew Batting Champion, All-Star outfielder Yordan Alvarez (.375, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 4 BB, 7 R, .708 SLG, .483 OBP) and first baseman Christian Walker (.348, 4 HR, 7 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 7 R, .913 SLG, .407 OBP); utilityman Luke Keaschall (.381, 1 HR, 6 RBI, 2 2B, 1 3B, 3 BB, 10 R, 1 SB, .905 SLG, .462 OBP) of the Minnesota Twins; closer Cade Smith (0.00 ERA, 3 G, 2 SV, 2.2 IP, 0 H, 1 BB, 4 SO) of the Cleveland Guardians; first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino (.333, 3 HR, 9 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 6 R, .792 SLG, .385 OBP) and outfielder Jac Caglianone (.455, 4 RBI, 5 2B, 4 R, .682 SLG, .455 OBP) of the Kansas City Royals; outfielder Wade Meckler (.435, 2 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 3 R, .565 SLG, .480 OBP) of the Los Angeles Angels; and All-Star first baseman Munetaka Murakami (.292, 3 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 2 BB, 5 R, .750 SLG, .370 OBP) and second baseman Chase Meidroth (.615, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 3 R, 1.000 SLG, .643 OBP) of the Chicago White Sox.
Atlanta Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. earned his fourth career Play of the Week Award, after previously winning on August 19, 2019; August 8, 2022; and July 21, 2025. Overall, it is the 13th honor for the Braves since the inception of the award in 2019 with Acuña’s four awards joined by honors to Charlie Culberson (7/8/2019); Nick Markakis (7/15/2019); Adam Duvall (9/8/2020); Tyler Matzek (5/10/2021); a joint award to Ozzie Albies and Orlando Arcia (7/3/2023); Austin Riley (8/19/2024); Michael Harris II (9/3/2024); Jurickson Profar (8/11/2025); and Jim Jarvis (5/11/2026). With no outs and the Braves leading the Marlins 1-0 in the second inning, Heriberto Hernández hit a ball towards the wall as Acuña made a leaping catch to take away extra-bases. Additional Play of the Week candidates included Javier Sanoja’s fantastic play to keep the game alive; Henry Bolte’s diving catch; Bryan Reynolds’ diving catch and throw to second for a double play; Ceddanne Rafaela’s diving catch; and Jase Bowen’s leaping catch at the wall.

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.
